The sound view is that this is the saying of one who is fair to his opponent while knowing that he is in error: he relates his words as they are, without being partisan to his own school, because that is more conducive to the truth and safer from confusion; then he turns back upon it after relating it and refutes it by argument. ﴿Then when it set﴾, i.e., disappeared, ﴿he said: I do not love those that set﴾, i.e., I do not love the worship of lords who change from one state to another, because that is among the attributes of bodies.

When he saw the moon rising, just beginning to appear, he said: "This is my lord." But when it set, he said: "If my Lord does not guide me, I shall surely be among the people who go astray." He thereby alerted his people that whoever takes the moon as a god is astray. He argued against them by its setting rather than its rising, though both are a movement from one state to another, because the argument from it is more evident: its setting is a movement accompanied by concealment and disappearance.

"When he saw the sun rising, he said, 'This is my Lord.'" Why did he use the masculine form (hadha, "this") here? Either because he intended the rising one (al-tali'), or because he made the subject like the predicate, since the two are one thing in meaning. And in it is the protection of the Lord from the suspicion of femininity. For this reason they said of the attributes of God the Exalted: "'Allam" (All-Knowing), and they did not say "'Allamah," even though the second would be more emphatic, to avoid the sign of femininity. "This is greater" is likewise an instance of using the attribute, also with his opponents. "So when it set, he said, 'O my people, I am free of what you associate [with God].'" That is, of the heavenly bodies that you make into partners of their Creator. It was also said: this was his reflection and his reasoning within himself, and God the Exalted related it. But the first is more apparent, because of his saying: "O my people, I am free of what you associate [with God]."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 79:

﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., toward the One whom these created things indicate as their Originator. ﴿Hanifan﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: inclining away from all religions except Islam. ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾, those who associate with Allah anything of His creation.

﴿His people argued with him﴾ concerning the Oneness of God, the Exalted, and the denial of partners to Him. ﴿He said: Do you argue with me about God﴾ concerning His Oneness? (The reading **أتُحاجُّونِي** [atuḥājjūnnī], with the final ي pronounced, is that of the Madani (the Medinan reader), and Ibn Dhakwan.) ﴿And He has guided me﴾ to the Oneness. The ي [in وَقَدْ هَدانِي] in continuous recitation (wasl) is read by Abu 'Amr.

When they frightened him that their deities would afflict him with harm, he said: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills anything﴾. That is: I never fear your deities at any time, because they have no power to benefit or harm, except when my Lord wills that they afflict me with harm. He is able to make benefit in whatever He wills and harm in whatever He wills; the idols are not. (p-518) ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, so no servant is struck by any harm or benefit except by His knowledge. ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ so that you may distinguish between the One who is able and the one who is powerless.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 81:

﴿And how should I fear what you associate[^1] with Him,﴾ [i.e., your deities,] which are safe from being feared; ﴿while you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down no authority upon you﴾ [i.e., no proof,] since association cannot have any proof behind it. The meaning is: what is the matter with you that you deny me security in a place of security, while you do not deny yourselves security in a place of fear? ﴿So which of the two parties﴾ [i.e., the party of the monotheists and the party of the polytheists] ﴿has more right to security﴾ from punishment ﴿if you know?﴾ He did not say "which of us," out of caution against praising himself. Then he began the answer to the question with His words:

[^1]: Arabic *ashraktum* (أشْرَكْتُمْ), from *shirk* (associating partners with God, a technical term in theology meaning polytheism or associationism).

"Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing (ẓulm)" — with shirk (association of partners with God). From al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him): "Those will have security, and they are guided." The words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) are complete here.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 83:

"And that was Our argument" (﴿وَتِلْكَ حُجَّتُنا﴾) is a reference to the whole of the argument that Abraham (peace be upon him) presented to his people, from his words ﴿When the night covered him﴾ up to ﴿and they are the ones guided﴾. ﴿We gave it to Abraham against his people﴾ is a statement following another statement. ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ in knowledge and wisdom. With tanwin (reading ḥujjatunā with nunation on the final letter, as a case of "dirhaman"?) is the reading of the Kufans. In it is a refutation of the view of the Mu'tazilah concerning al-aslah (what is most beneficial for the servant).

﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise﴾, with the raf' (nominative vowel on the word "Wise"), read as ḥakīmun.

﴿Knowing﴾, with regard to the people (al-ahl, the ones deserving of such rank).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 84:

﴿And We bestowed upon him﴾ (Ibrahim),

﴿Ishaq and Ya'qub; each of them We guided﴾. That is: all of them (p-519). Kullan (each of them) is in the accusative, governed by hadayna (We guided). ﴿And Nuh We guided﴾, that is: and We guided Nuh ﴿before﴾, i.e., before Ibrahim, ﴿and among his descendants﴾. The pronoun in dhurriyyatihi (his descendants) refers to Nuh or to Ibrahim, and the first is more apparent, because Yunus (Jonah) and Lut (Lot) were not among the descendants of Ibrahim. ﴿Dawud (David), Sulayman (Solomon), Ayyub (Job), Yusuf (Joseph), Musa (Moses) and Harun (Aaron)﴾. The implied meaning is: We guided from among his descendants these persons. ﴿And thus do We reward the good-doers﴾. And We reward the good-doers with a reward like that. So the kaf (thus) in its position is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar).

ۗ **[Verse 85]** "And Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Ilyas — all of them" (كُلٌّ):

﴿وَزَكَرِيّا ويَحْيى وعِيسى وإلْياسَ كُلٌّ﴾ — i.e., all of them — ﴿مِنَ الصالِحِينَ﴾ "were of the righteous."

The mention of 'Isa along with them is evidence that lineage is also established through the mother, because He (Allah) attributed him to the offspring of Nuh, peace be upon him, and he is not connected to him except through the mother. It is on this basis that al-Hajjaj was answered when he denied that the sons of Fatima were the sons of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And Ishmael and Elisha﴾ (*wa-l-Laysa'a*, with two *lam*s, *wa-al-Laysa'a*), where it is read with two *lam*s by Hamza and Ali.

﴿And Jonah and Lot, and all of them We preferred over the worlds﴾ by prophethood and messengerhood.

Translation of al-Nasafi's commentary on Surah 6, verse 87:

﴿And of their fathers﴾ is in the accusative position, conjoined to "kullan" (each one), meaning: and We preferred some of their fathers ﴿and their offspring and their brothers. We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾.

**﴿Dhalika﴾** means: what these people mentioned were following.

**﴿Hudā Allāh﴾** is the religion of God. **﴿Yahdī bihi man yashā'u min 'ibādihi﴾** — in this there is a refutation of the saying of the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites), for they say: God willed the guidance of all creation, but they were not guided.

**﴿Wa-law ashrakū﴾** — despite their excellence, their precedence, and the lofty ranks God raised them to — **﴿la-ḥabiṭa 'anhum mā kānū ya'malūn﴾**: their deeds would have been nullified, as He said: **﴿La-in ashraktA la-yaḥbaṭanna 'amaluka﴾** [al-Zumar: 65] ("If you were to associate partners with God, your deeds would surely be nullified").

﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾ means the category (al-jins), ﴿and the judgment﴾ and wisdom, or the understanding of the Book, ﴿and prophethood﴾, which is the highest rank of humankind. ﴿If they disbelieve in them﴾, that is, in the Book, the judgment, and the prophethood, or in the verses of the Qur'an, ﴿these﴾, that is, the people of Makkah.

﴿Then We have entrusted with them a people﴾. They are the prophets mentioned, and those who followed them, based on His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ (6:90). Or they are the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), or everyone who believed in him, or the ʿajam (non-Arabs). The meaning of entrusting them with it is that they were granted success in believing in it and in upholding its rights, just as a man is entrusted with a thing so that he will attend to it, look after it, and guard it. The bāʾ (ب) in ﴿laysū bihā﴾ (لَيْسُوا بِها) is a ṣila (a particle that completes the meaning of the governing word), attached to kāfirīn (كافِرِينَ, "disbelievers"), while the bāʾ in ﴿bi-kāfirīn﴾ (بِكافِرِينَ) serves to emphasize the negation.

(p-٥٢٠)

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided﴾, that is, the prophets whose mention has passed. ﴿So follow their guidance﴾: their guidance is singled out for following, and you should follow none but them. This is the meaning of fronting the object (*taqdim al-maf'ul*, placing the object before the verb). By "their guidance" is meant their way in belief in Allah, in His unity (*tawhid*), and in the fundamentals of the religion, not the legal rulings (*shara'i*), which differ. The *ha'* in *iqtadih* is for pausing (*waqf*, stopping at the end of a word) and is dropped in continuous recitation (*wasl*, joining words). He considered preferring the pause to be good, because the *ha'* is retained in the *mushaf* (the written codex). Hamzah and Ali omit it in continuous recitation, and the Shami reader pronounces it with *ikhtilas* (a rapid, truncated articulation of the vowel).

﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it﴾, for the revelation, or for conveying the message and calling to the Oneness of Allah.

﴿Any reward﴾: a wage (*ju'l*, payment). In this there is evidence that taking payment for teaching the Qur'an and for transmitting hadith is impermissible. ﴿It is nothing but a reminder for the worlds﴾: the Qur'an is nothing but an admonition for jinn and humankind.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 6, verse 91:**

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being."﴾ That is, they did not know Him with His true knowledge regarding His mercy toward His servants, when they denied the sending of messengers and the revelation to them. This is among the greatest of His mercies. ﴿We have sent you not but as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. It is narrated that a group of Jews, among them Malik ibn al-Sayf, used to argue with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Is it not in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?" He said, "Yes." He said, "You are the fat rabbi." (p-521) So he became angry and said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being." And ﴿ḥaqqa qadrihi﴾ (حَقَّ قَدْرِهِ) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (naṣb al-maṣdar, the accusative of the infinitive, indicating the manner of the action). ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought as a light﴾ — "as a light" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring either to the pronoun in "bihi" (with it) or to "al-Kitab" (the Book). ﴿and a guidance for people, which you make into scrolls, displaying them while concealing much﴾ — concealing, from what it contains of the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). That is, they broke it up and made it into separate scrolls and scattered sheets, so that they could carry out what they intended of displaying and concealing. The reading with the yā' (يَ, third person) in all three verbs ("yubdūnahā", "yukhfūna", and the related verb) is that of Makki and Abu 'Amr.

﴿And you were taught﴾ — O People of the Book — through the Book ﴿what neither you nor your fathers knew﴾ of the matters of your religion and your worldly affairs. ﴿Say: God﴾ — this is the answer; that is, God sent it down. They are not able to deny you. ﴿Then leave them in their idle talk﴾ — in their falsehood in which they plunge ﴿playing﴾ — a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring either to "dharhum" (leave them) or to "khawḍihim" (their plunging).

This is a Book We have sent down (to Our Prophet (ﷺ)), blessed, abounding in benefits and advantages, confirming that which came before it of the Books, and that you may warn the Mother of the Cities (Makkah). It was called Umm al-Qura because it is the navel of the earth, the qiblah (direction of prayer) of the people of the towns, the greatest of them in standing, and because people turn toward it. And those around it, the people of the East and the West. And those who believe in the Hereafter, who affirm the outcome and fear it, believe in it, that is, in this Book. The basis of religion is fear of the outcome, so whoever fears it, fear does not leave him until he believes. And they are over their prayer they guard. Prayer was singled out for mention because it is the sign of faith and the pillar of religion, so whoever guards it guards its counterparts outwardly.

*Note on the recitation:* وَلِتُنْذِرَ with the ya' (وَلِيُنْذِرَ) is the reading of Abu Bakr, meaning "and that it may warn," with the Book as the subject. This is conjoined to what the attribute of the Book implies, as if it had been said: We sent it down for blessings, for confirming what preceded it of the Books, and for warning Umm al-Qura.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 93:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who fabricates a lie against Allah,﴾ this is Malik ibn al-Sayf, ﴿or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him,﴾ this is Musaylima the Liar. ﴿And one who says,﴾ in a position of genitive conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿one who fabricates﴾, meaning: "and of those who say," ﴿"I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down,"﴾ meaning: "I will say and dictate," this is ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, the scribe of the revelation (katib al-wahy). The Prophet ﷺ had dictated to him: ﴿And indeed We created man from an extract of clay...﴾ up to ﴿another creation.﴾ Then there flowed from his tongue: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾ The Prophet said, "Write it down, for thus was it revealed." He then doubted and said, "If Muhammad is truthful, then it has been revealed to me just as it was revealed to him, and if he is lying, then I have said just as he said." So he apostatized and joined Mecca. Or it was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to say: "By those who grind with a grinding, then those who knead with a kneading, then those who bake with a baking," as if he were competing (with the Qur'an).

﴿And if you could see﴾ its answer is omitted, meaning: "you would see a terrifying matter."

﴿When the wrongdoers﴾ means those whom he mentioned from among the Jews and the false prophets, in which case the definite article (al-) is for prior reference (ʿahd). It is also permissible for it to be for the category (jins), so that these people enter into it because of its comprehensiveness. ﴿are in the agonies of death﴾, its hardships and its death-throes.

﴿while the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation"﴾ meaning: they extend their hands to them, saying, "Bring out your spirits; bring them out to us from your bodies." This is an expression for severity in taking the soul without respite or delay. ﴿They are recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ meaning the time of death and what they are tormented with of the severity of the extraction. Al-hun is intense humiliation. The attribution of the punishment to it is like your saying "a man of evil" (rajul su'), meaning: deep-rootedness in humiliation and being firmly established in it. ﴿for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth﴾ — that He has a partner, a consort, and a son. "Ghayr al-haqq" is the object of ﴿say﴾, or a descriptor of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a saying other than the truth. ﴿And you used to be arrogant toward His signs﴾, so they would not believe in them.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 94:**

﴿And you have certainly come to Us﴾ for the reckoning and the recompense, ﴿alone (furada)﴾, individually, without wealth and without any helper. Furada is the plural of farid, like asir and usara (prisoners).

﴿As We created you﴾ is in the accusative position as an adjective of the verbal noun of "you have come to Us", meaning: a coming like the way We created you ﴿the first time﴾, in the states in which you were born, alone. ﴿And you left behind what We had bestowed upon you﴾, what We had made you possess, ﴿behind your backs﴾, and you did not carry from it a speck. ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be partners in your worship﴾ of Him. ﴿Your connection has been severed between you (baynakum)﴾, your bond, according to al-Zajjaj. Al-bayn means the joining and the separation. He said:

*By Allah, were it not for separation, desire would not exist,*
*and were it not for desire, the one accustomed would not long for separation.*

The reading (baynakum) is from Madani, Ali and Hafs, meaning: the severance has occurred between you. ﴿And what you used to claim has strayed from you﴾ and been lost and become void, that they were your intercessors with Allah.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 95:**

﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾, with the vegetation and the trees. That is, He splits the grain from its ear (sunbula) and the date-stone from the palm tree. Al-falq (splitting) means cleaving. It is reported from Mujahid that he meant the two parts (shaqqayn) that are in the date-stone and in the wheat.

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾: the tender, growing plant out of the dry grain. ﴿And He brings the dead out of the living﴾: the dry grain out of the growing plant; or a human being out of a drop of semen, and a drop of semen out of a human being; or a believer out of an unbeliever, and an unbeliever out of a believer. Allah thus argued against them with what they witness of His creation, because they denied the resurrection. So He informed them that He is the One who created these things, and so He is able to resurrect them.

He said ﴿mukhriju al-mayyit﴾ (the one who brings out the dead) in the form of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), because it is coordinated with fali'q al-habb (the splitter of the grain), not with the verb. The phrase ﴿yukhriju al-hayy min al-mayyit﴾ (He brings the living out of the dead) stands in the position of a clause explaining His words ﴿fali'q al-habb wa'l-nawa﴾ (the splitter of the grain and the date-stone), because the splitting of the grain and the date-stone to produce the growing plants and trees is of the same kind as bringing the living out of the dead, since the growing thing is in the ruling of the living being. The proof of this is His saying ﴿and He gives life to the earth after its death﴾.

﴿That is Allah﴾: that One who gives life and causes death is Allah, the One who alone deserves lordship (al-rububiyyah), not the idols. ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ That is, how are you diverted from Him, and from turning to other than Him, after the matter has become clear through what we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 96:

﴿Fāliq al-iṣbāḥ﴾ (the Cleaver of the dawn) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a name for the dawn (al-ṣubḥ), meaning: the one who splits the column of dawn (ʿamūd al-ṣubḥ) from the blackness of the night. Or it means: the Creator of the light of day. ﴿Wa-jaʿala al-layl﴾ (and He made the night): this reading is that of the Kufans (Kūfī), because the active participle (ism al-fāʿil) that precedes it has the sense of the past tense (al-muḍiyy). Since fāliq carries the meaning of faláqa (He split), He coordinated with it jaʿala, so that the two agree in meaning. ﴿Sakanan﴾ (a place of rest) means something in which one rests, from His saying: ﴿that you may rest therein﴾ [Yunus: 67]. That is: so that creatures may rest in it from the toil of livelihood into the sleep of heedlessness, or from the loneliness of creatures into intimacy with the Truth.

﴿Wa-al-shamsa wa-al-qamar﴾ (and the sun and the moon) are in the accusative by virtue of a verb implied by "jāʿil al-layl" (the Maker of the night), meaning: and He made the sun and the moon ﴿ḥusbānan﴾ (a reckoning). That is: He made them according to a reckoning, because the calculation of times is known by their orbit and their course. Ḥusbān with a ḍammah is a verbal noun of ḥasaba (to reckon), just as ḥisbān with a kasrah is a verbal noun of ḥasiba (to suppose). ﴿Dhālika﴾ (that) refers to their being made a reckoning; that is: that ordering by a known computation ﴿is the decree of the Mighty﴾ who subdued them and subjected them ﴿the Knowing﴾ in arranging them and in their revolving.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 97:**

﴿And it is He who made for you the stars﴾ — He created them — ﴿that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾ — i.e., in the darknesses of the night, on land and at sea. He attributed them (the darknesses) to these two because they are associated with them. Or he likened the confusing paths to darknesses. ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ — We have made clear the signs that point to the Oneness (tawhid) for a people who know.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 98:

﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul﴾; it is Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿So there is a place of stability and a place of storage﴾. (Fa-mustaqarrun) with a kasra [on the qaf] is the reading of Ibn Kathir (Makki) and Basri [i.e., Abu 'Amr]. Whoever reads the qaf with a fatha, then al-mustawda' is a noun of place in the same pattern; whoever reads it with a kasra, then it is an active participle, and al-mustawda' is a passive participle. The meaning: for you there is a stability in the womb and a storage in the loins; or a stability above the earth and a storage beneath it. Or: among you there is one who is stable and among you one who is stored. ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾. The reason it was said "they know" (ya'lamun) earlier, and "understand" (yafqahun) here, is that the indication there is more evident, whereas here it is subtler, because the production of mankind from a single soul, and their being moved between different states, is subtler. So the mention of fiqh (understanding), which indicates refinement of reflection, was more appropriate.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 99:

﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky﴾: that is, rain from the clouds. ﴿And We brought forth thereby﴾: by means of the water, ﴿the growth of every thing﴾: the growth of every kind among the kinds of things that grow. That is: the cause is one, namely water, while the things caused are of various kinds. ﴿Then We brought forth from it﴾: from the vegetation,

﴿green﴾: that is, something fresh and green. It is said: akhdar and khadir (both meaning green), and it is what branches out from the root of the plant emerging from the seed. ﴿We bring forth from it﴾: from the green, ﴿grain piled up﴾: this is the ear of grain whose grains are layered upon one another. ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters﴾: this is in the nominative as the subject of the sentence, and "min al-nakhli" (from the palm trees) is its predicate. ﴿From their spathes﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it, as if it had been said: and there are clusters produced from the spathes of the palm tree. It is the plural of qinw, which is the cluster of dates (idhq), and its parallel is sinw and sinwan.

﴿Hanging low﴾: within reach for picking, either because they bend under the weight of their load, or because their stems are short. This is an instance of ellipsis (iktifa'), meaning: and others are not hanging low because they are tall, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. ﴿And gardens﴾: in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿the growth of every thing﴾; that is, and We brought forth by it gardens ﴿of grapes﴾, that is, along with the palm trees. Likewise: ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾. (And gardens) in the nominative: al-A'sha's reading, meaning: and there are gardens of grapes, that is, along with the palm trees. ﴿Similar and dissimilar﴾: it is said: "ashtabaha al-shay'an" and "tashabaha" (the two things became alike), like "istawaya" and "tasawaya" (they became equal). The pattern ifti'al and tafa'ul often share meaning. Its implied sense is: and the olive similar and dissimilar, and the pomegranate likewise; that is, some of it is similar and some dissimilar in size, colour and taste.

﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾: when it brings forth its fruit, how it brings it out weak, of no benefit, ﴿and its ripening﴾ and its maturity; that is, look at its ripening, how it returns to become something combining many benefits. It is a look of contemplation and reasoning on the power of the One who ordains it, manages it, and moves it from one state to another. ﴿Surely in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ (Thumurihi): Hamzah and Ali (read it so), and likewise what follows. It is the plural of thimar, so it is the plural of a plural. It is said: thamara, thamar, thimar, and thumur (all forms of the word for fruit).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 100:

﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾. If you take ﴿partners for God﴾ as the two objects of "made" (ja'ala), then "the jinn" (al-jinn) is an apposition (badal) to "partners." Otherwise, ﴿partners the jinn﴾ are two objects, with the second placed before the first. The purpose of the fronting is to magnify the idea that anyone should be taken as a partner of God, whether he be an angel, a jinn, or something else. The meaning is: they obeyed the jinn in what the jinn embellished for them of their polytheism, so they made them partners with God. ﴿And He created them﴾, that is, while He is the One who created the jinn, how can the created be a partner to its Creator? This clause is a circumstantial clause (hal), or it means: and He created those who make partners with God, so how can they worship other than Him? ﴿And they invented for Him﴾, that is, they fabricated. It is said: he "khalaqa al-ifk," "kharaqahu," "ikhtalaqahu," and "ikhtarakahu," with the same meaning; or it is from "kharaqa al-thawb" (he tore the garment) when he tore it, that is, they tore out for Him ﴿sons﴾, like the saying of the People of the Two Books regarding the Messiah and 'Uzayr, ﴿and daughters﴾, like the saying of some of the Arabs regarding the angels. (And "kharraqu") with the doubled letter for intensification is from Madani, due to His saying: ﴿sons and daughters﴾. ﴿Without knowledge﴾, without them knowing the reality of what they said, whether it was wrong or right, but casting a saying out of ignorance. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "kharaqu," that is, they were ignorant of what they said. ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted is He above what they describe﴾, of partner and offspring.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 101:

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. It is said: "badaʿa al-shayʾ" (he originated the thing), so it is "badīʿ" (originator/wondrous). This is from the idafa (genitive construction) of the attributive adjective (al-sifa al-mushabbaha) to its agent, meaning: "badīʿ samawātihi wa arḍihi" (the originator of His heavens and His earth). Or it is in the sense of "al-mubdiʿ" (the one who originates), i.e., "mubdiʿuhā" (its originator). It is either the predicate of a deleted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), or a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿How could He have a child﴾. Or it is the agent (fa'il) of "taʿalā" (exalted is He).

﴿And He has no consort﴾, i.e., from where could He have a child? A child can only come from a consort, and He has no consort! That is: begetting is one of the attributes of bodies, and the originator of bodies cannot be a body so as to have a child.

﴿And He created all things, and He is All-Knowing of all things﴾, i.e., there is nothing except that He is its creator and its knower. Whoever is like this is free of need from everything, and a child is only sought by one who is in need.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 102:

﴿That is﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the one described by the attributes mentioned before. It is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it are predicates in succession (akhbar mutaradifah), namely: ﴿Allah is your Lord; there is no god but He, the Creator of everything﴾. His saying ﴿so worship Him﴾ is a consequence (musabbab) of the meaning of the sentence, i.e., whoever has all these attributes gathered in him is the one truly deserving of worship, so worship Him, and do not worship anyone other than Him from among His creatures. ﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾, i.e., He, along with those attributes, is the owner of everything in terms of provisions and lifespans, and the watcher over deeds.

﴿Eyes cannot perceive Him﴾: meaning, they cannot encompass Him. Or it means the eyes of those previously mentioned. The Mu'tazila's (the rationalist school that denied the vision of God in the Hereafter) reliance on this verse does not hold, because what is negated is *idrak* (comprehension), not *ru'ya* (seeing). *Idrak* means standing at the limits and boundaries of the seen thing. Whatever is impossible for limits and directions to apply to is impossible to comprehend, but not impossible to see. So comprehension is related to seeing as encompassment (*ihata*) is related to knowledge. Negating encompassment, which entails standing at the limits and boundaries, does not entail negating knowledge of Him. So it is with this. Moreover, the context of the verse, which is praise, requires the affirmation of seeing. For negating the comprehension of what cannot be seen carries no praise, since everything that is not seen is not comprehended. The praise lies only in negating comprehension while affirming seeing, for its negation alongside the realization of seeing is a sign of the removal of the deficiency of finitude and limits from the Essence. Thus the verse is a proof for us against them. Had they reflected on it carefully, they would have seized the opportunity to be free of its burden. Whoever negates seeing is necessarily obliged to negate that He is known and existent. Otherwise, just as He is known to exist without modality or direction, unlike every existent, why would it not be permissible for Him to be seen without modality or direction, unlike every seen thing? This is because seeing is the realization of a thing by sight as it is. If the seen object is in a direction, it is seen in that direction; and if it is not in a direction, it is seen without being in one. ﴿And He﴾, for the subtlety of His perception, ﴿perceives the eyes; and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾: that is, the One who knows the fine details of matters and their intricacies.

﴿the All-Aware﴾: the Knowing of the apparent aspects of things and their hidden aspects. This is of the type of *laff wa-nashr* (a rhetorical device of wrapping and unfolding, where multiple items are mentioned and then their correspondents are given in order).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 104:

﴿Indeed there has come to you insights (baṣā'ir) from your Lord.﴾ Al-baṣīrah (insight) is the light of the heart by which the heart gains insight, just as al-baṣar (sight) is the light of the eye by which you see. That is: there has come to you from the revelation and the admonition that which is for the hearts like insights (baṣā'ir). ﴿So whoever sees﴾ the truth and believes, ﴿it is for his own self that he sees﴾, and it is to his own benefit that he has profited. ﴿And whoever is blind﴾ to it and goes astray, ﴿then it is against himself﴾, so he has blinded himself, and to his own self he has done harm by the blindness. ﴿And I am not a watcher over you﴾, I do not guard your deeds and I do not requite you for them. I am only a warner, and Allah is the Watcher over you.

The kaf in ﴿Thus do We vary the verses﴾ is in the accusative position as an adjective (ṣifah) of the omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: We vary the verses in a variation like what We have recited to you. ﴿And so that they say﴾: its response (jawab) is omitted, meaning: and so that they say, ﴿"You have studied"﴾ — We vary them. The meaning of ﴿"You have studied"﴾ is "you have read the books of the People of the Book."

(Dārasat) is read by Makkī and Abū ʿAmr, meaning: they have studied with the People of the Book. (Darasat) is read by al-Shāmī, meaning: this verse has been preceded and has passed, as they said, "tales of the ancients."

﴿And that We may make it clear﴾: "it" refers to the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned before, because it is known; or it refers to the verses, since they carry the meaning of the Qur'an. It has been said: the second lam is causal (ḥaqīqah, genuine), and the first lam is the lam of consequence and outcome (lam al-ʿāqibah wa al-ṣayrūrah), meaning: so that the outcome of their affair becomes that they say "You have studied." This is like your saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], though they did not pick him up for enmity; they picked him up so that he would become a delight of the eye for them, but the outcome of their affair became enmity. Likewise, the verses were varied for the sake of clarification, and were not varied so that they would say "You have studied"; rather, this saying resulted from the variation of the verses, just as clarification resulted, and so it was likened to it. It has also been said that "so that they say" is like "so that We may make it clear." According to us, it is not so, because of what is known: ﴿for a people who know﴾ the truth from falsehood.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 106:

﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord.﴾ And do not follow their desires. ﴿There is no deity except Him.﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (i‘tiraD), used to emphasize the obligation to follow the revelation, and it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "your Lord," serving as an emphasis.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾ for the time being, until the command to fight arrives.

(p-529)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 107:

﴿And had Allah willed﴾, i.e., their faith, so the object is omitted.

﴿They would not have associated⦆ shows that they do not associate (others with Allah) against the will of Allah. Had He known from them a choice of accepting faith, He would have guided them to it, but He knew from them a choice of association, so He willed their association, and they associated by His will. ﴿We did not make you a guardian over them﴾, one who watches over their deeds or holds them accountable for their sins. ﴿Nor are you a guardian over them﴾, one with authority over them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 108:

The Muslims used to revile their gods, so they were forbidden, lest their reviling become a cause for reviling Allah, by His saying: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge.﴾ The word ﴿enmity﴾ is in the accusative as a response to the prohibition (ʿalā jawāb al-nahy, i.e., an answer to the negative command). ﴿Enmity﴾ means injustice and transgression. ﴿Without knowledge﴾ means out of ignorance of Allah and of what is due to be mentioned concerning Him. ﴿Thus﴾ means like that adornment, ﴿We have made attractive to every community﴾ among the communities of the disbelievers ﴿their deeds﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good [equal to one who is rightly guided]? For indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8]. And it is a proof for us regarding what is best (al-aslah).

﴿Then to their Lord is their return﴾, that is, their destination, ﴿and He will inform them of what they used to do﴾, that is, He will tell them of what they did and will recompense them for it.

ﷻ "And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths" — ﴿وَأقْسَمُوا بِاللهِ جَهْدَ أيْمانِهِمْ﴾

Jahd (جَهْدَ) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) occupying the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: striving in bringing the most emphatic of oaths. ﴿Should a sign come to them﴾ from among their proposed signs, ﴿they will surely believe in it.﴾ Say: ﴿The signs are only with Allah﴾, and He is able to produce them, not I; so how could I bring them to you? ﴿And what will make you realise﴾ — meaning, what will inform you — ﴿that when it comes they will not believe﴾ in it? That is: I know that when that proposed sign comes they will not believe in it, while you do not know this.

The believers used to hope that they would believe if that sign came, and they wished for its coming. So Allah, exalted is He, said: "And what will make you realise that they will not believe?" — meaning: you do not know what has already preceded in My knowledge, that they will not believe.

(إنَّها) with a kasra — Makki, Basri, and Abu Bakr, on the basis that the speech was complete before it, meaning: "And what will make you realise what will happen from them?" Then He informed them of His knowledge concerning them, saying: "Indeed, when it comes, they will absolutely not believe." Among them, some considered "lā" (لا) to be extra (zā'idah) in the reading with a fatḥa, like His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 95]. (لا تُؤْمِنُونَ) — Shami and Hamza.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 110:

﴿And We turn their hearts⁠ away from accepting the truth and their eyes⁠ away from seeing the truth⁠ at the descent of the sign they demanded, so they do not believe in it.⁠﴾ It has been said: this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿they do not believe﴾, falling under the ruling of ﴿And what will make you realize⁠﴾, meaning: and what will make you realize that they do not believe, and what will make you realize that We turn their hearts and their eyes, so that they do not comprehend and do not perceive the truth,

﴿just as they did not believe in it the first time⁠﴾, just as they, at the descent of Our signs initially, did not believe in them, ﴿and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly⁠﴾. It has been said: and what will make you realize that We leave them in their transgression, wandering in confusion?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 111:

﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, as they said: "Why have the angels not been sent down to us?" ﴿and the dead had spoken to them﴾, as they said: "Then bring our forefathers [back to life]."

﴿And We gathered against them﴾, i.e., We assembled, ﴿every thing face to face﴾ (qubulan), as guarantors of the truth of what We gave good tidings of and warned against. It is the plural of qabil, which means guarantor (kafil). (Qubulan) is read by the people of Medina and by the Syrian reader, meaning "in plain sight" (ʿiyanan). Both readings are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿They would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ their belief, so that they would believe. This is a response to the statement of the believers: "Perhaps they will believe when the sign comes down."

﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾ that these people will not believe when the proposed sign comes to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 112:

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾ Just as We have appointed for you enemies from among the polytheists, We have appointed for those who preceded you among the prophets enemies, because of what there is in it of trial (ibtila'), which is the cause of the manifestation of steadfastness (thabat), patience (sabr), and the abundance of reward (thawab) and recompense (ajr). The words ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ are in the accusative either as a substitute (badal) for "enemy" or as the first object (maf'ul awwal), with "enemy" being the second object (maf'ul thani). (p-531) ﴿Inspiring one another﴾ means: the devils of the jinn whisper to the devils of mankind, and likewise some of the jinn to others, and some of mankind to others.

It is related from Malik ibn Dinar that he said: "The devil of mankind is harsher upon me than the devil of the jinn, for when I seek refuge in Allah, the devil of the jinn leaves me, but the devil of mankind comes to me and drags me openly into sins."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Evil companions are worse than the devils of the jinn."

﴿Embellished speech (zukhruf al-qawl)﴾ means what they have adorned of speech, whispering, and incitement to sins. ﴿Deception (ghurur)﴾ means deceit and seizing [someone] unawares; it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ that is, the inspiring. The meaning is: had Allah willed, He would have prevented the devils from whispering, but He tested [people] with what He knows to be greater in reward. ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ against you and against Allah; for Allah will disgrace them, grant you victory, and recompense them.

And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it (the embellished speech); and that the hearts of the disbelievers may be inclined to the ornamented word. It is coordinated with "ghurūran" (as deception), meaning: so that they may deceive him. ﴿And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ ﴿and that they may be pleased with it﴾ for themselves ﴿and that they may commit what they are committing﴾ of sins.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 114:

﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ That is: Say, O Muhammad, "Shall I seek a judge other than Allah, who will judge between me and you and will separate the one who is right from us from the one who is in falsehood?" ﴿And it is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, the inimitable (al-mu'jiz), ﴿detailed﴾ (mufassalan). This is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Book," meaning: clarified within it is the distinction between truth and falsehood, and the testimony in my favour regarding truthfulness, and against you regarding fabrication. Then he reinforced the proof that the Qur'an is true by the knowledge of the People of the Book that it is true, because of its confirmation of what they possess and its agreement with it.

﴿And those to whom We have given the Book﴾, that is: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, ﴿know that it is sent down﴾ (yaʿlamūna annahu munazzalun). Read by Ibn ʿAmir (Shami) and Hafs.

﴿from your Lord in truth. So do not be among those who doubt﴾ (al-mumtarin), the skeptics about it, O listener, (p-532) or: ﴿do not be among those who doubt﴾ concerning the fact that the People of the Book know that it is sent down in truth; and let not the denial of most of them, and their disbelief in it, trouble you.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 115:**

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾, i.e., what He has spoken. (*Kalimatu rabbika*, "the words of your Lord") is the reading of the people of the Hijaz, the Syrians, and Abu 'Amr. That is: all that He has informed of, commanded, forbade, promised, and threatened has been fulfilled.

﴿in truth﴾ regarding His promise and His threat, ﴿and justice﴾ regarding His command and His prohibition. Both words are in the accusative, either as a *tamyiz* (specification, "in respect of truth and justice") or as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier, "truthful and just"). ﴿None can alter His words﴾, meaning no one can change anything of that. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the affirmation of whoever affirms, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of the persistence of whoever persists; or, He is the All-Hearing of what they say and the All-Knowing of what they conceal.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 116:

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, because they are the majority, ﴿they will lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾, i.e., His religion, ﴿they follow nothing but conjecture (ẓann)﴾, and this conjecture is their assumption that their forefathers were upon the truth, so they imitate them (taqlid), ﴿and they are only guessing (yakhrusun)﴾, lying about Allah having forbidden for them such-and-such, and made lawful for them such-and-such.

Qur'anic verse 117 of Surah al-An'am: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ Meaning: He knows the disbelievers and the believers.

"Man" (مَن) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and its form is that of an interrogative, while the predicate (khabar) is "yadillu" (yaḍillu, "he strays"). The position of the clause is in the accusative case, governed by the implied verb "ya'lamu" (yaʿlamu, "He knows"), not by the imperative "a'lam" (aʿlam, "know"), because the form af'ala (ʾafʿala, the comparative/elative form) does not govern an explicit noun in the accusative, but governs the genitive (jarr). It has been said that its implied form is: "a'lamu bi-man yadillu" (aʿlamu biman yaḍillu, "I know best of whom strays"), as evidence by the appearance of the preposition bi (bi, "with/of") after it in "bil-muhtadin" (bilmuhtadīn, "of those who are guided").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 118:

﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been pronounced, if you are believers in His revelations.﴾ This is a consequence of the denial of following the misguiders who make lawful what is forbidden and forbid what is lawful. That is because they used to say to the Muslims: "You claim that you worship Allah; so what Allah has killed is more deserving that you eat what you have killed yourselves." So it was said to the Muslims: "If you are truly established in faith, then eat of that over which the name of Allah has been pronounced" (p-533) specifically, that is, over its slaughter, and not that over which the name of others than Him, from their gods, has been pronounced, or that which died a natural death.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 119:

﴿And what is it with you that you do not eat﴾ "Ma" is an interrogative in a position of raising (nominative) as the subject of the sentence (mubtada'), and "lakum" (for you) is the predicate (khabar). That is: "And what purpose do you have in not eating﴾ ﴿of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, while He has already explained to you﴾ made clear to you.

﴿what He has forbidden to you﴾ of what has not been forbidden, by His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. "Fussila" and "hurrima" are read by Kufi (readers other than Hafs) with the first vowel marked as in the pattern of passive verbs; with an open vowel on both by Madani and Hafs; and with a damma on both by the others.

﴿except what you are compelled to﴾ of what has been forbidden to you, for it is lawful for you in a state of necessity, that is, the severity of hunger that compels you to eat it. ﴿And indeed many lead astray﴾ "liyudillūna" (with a different vowelling) per Kufi,

﴿by their desires without knowledge﴾ That is: they go astray, so they forbid and permit by their own whims and desires, without adherence to any revealed law. ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the truth into falsehood.

﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin﴾: its open and its secret. Or, fornication in the shops (al-hawanit), and illicit companionship (al-sadiqa) in secret. Or, open and hidden shirk.

﴿Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿for what they used to commit﴾, that is, what they used to acquire in this world.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 121:**

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, at the time of slaughter.

﴿And indeed it is﴾, meaning that eating it is ﴿grave disobedience (fisq)﴾. ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire﴾, meaning they whisper ﴿to their allies﴾ among the polytheists ﴿to dispute with you﴾ by their saying: "You do not eat what Allah has killed, but you eat what you slaughter with your own hands!" The verse prohibits what was left without the mention of God's name. The case of forgetting is excepted by the hadith, or the forgetful person is treated as one who remembers, by implicit assumption.

﴿And if you obey them﴾ in making lawful what Allah has forbidden, ﴿indeed you are polytheists﴾, because whoever follows other than Allah in his religion has associated partners with Him. It is incumbent on one who is religiously committed not to eat what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over, because of the great severity contained in the verse. The beginning of the verse is connected with carrion, and with what has been dedicated to other than Allah, based on His saying: ﴿or a grave sin, over which a name other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-An'am: 145].

He said: The "wa" in ﴿and indeed it is grave disobedience﴾ is for the circumstantial clause (hal), because conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal one is not good usage. So the meaning is: "And do not eat of it while it is grave disobedience." Grave disobedience (fisq) is general, so it is clarified by His saying: ﴿or a grave sin, over which a name other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. Thus the meaning becomes: "And do not eat of it while it has been dedicated to other than Allah," so whatever else is lawful by the general rules that make things lawful, among them His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find﴾ the verse [al-An'am: 145]. He has thereby departed from the apparent wording of the text.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 122:

﴿Is he who was dead and We brought him to life﴾, i.e., disbelieving, and We guided him, because faith is the life of the hearts. ("Maytan," dead) is read by Madani (Ibn Kathir? no: the Madani reading) ... [see note below] ﴿and made for him a light by which he walks among the people﴾, illuminated by it, and what is meant by it is certainty (yaqin).

﴿like one whose likeness﴾, i.e., description, ﴿is in the darknesses﴾, i.e., wallowing in them, ﴿not coming out of them﴾, not parting from them and not freeing himself from them. This is a circumstantial clause (hal). It was said: what is meant by the two are Hamzah and Abu Jahl, but the more correct view is that the verse is general to everyone whom God has guided and everyone whom God has misguided. So it clarifies that the likeness of the one who is guided is the likeness of the dead man who was brought to life and made illuminated, walking among the people by the light of wisdom and faith, and the likeness of the disbeliever is the likeness of one who is in darknesses from which he cannot free himself. ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., just as his faith was made attractive to the believer, ﴿it was made attractive to the disbelievers﴾ by God's making it attractive, as in His saying: ﴿We made their deeds attractive to them﴾ [An-Naml: 4] ﴿what they used to do﴾, i.e., their deeds.

**[Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 6, verse 123]**

﴿And thus﴾, that is: just as We placed in Makkah its chieftains so that they would scheme therein, ﴿We placed﴾, We made, ﴿in every town the greatest of its criminals so that they would scheme therein﴾, so that they would tyrannize over the people there and engage in acts of disobedience. The lam (ل) in ﴿لِيَمْكُرُوا﴾ is according to the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) on its apparent meaning, and it is not the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). He singled out the greatest (al-akabir), who are the leaders, because the leadership and abundance they possess make them more inclined to scheming and disbelief than others. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿If Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely transgress upon the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 27]. Then He consoled His Messenger (ﷺ) and promised him support.

﴿And they scheme only against themselves﴾, because their scheming rebounds upon them, ﴿and they do not perceive it﴾ that it rebounds upon them.

"Akabir" (أكابِرَ) is the first object (maf'ul awwal), and the second is: ﴿in every town﴾. And "mujrimiha" (مُجْرِمِيها) is a substitute (badal) for "akabir." Or the first is "mujrimiha," and the second is "akabir," and the implied construction is: "mujrimiha akabir" (its criminals, the greatest of them).

When Abu Jahl said: "The sons of ʿAbd Manaf have vied with us for nobility, until we became like two racehorses in a contest. They say: 'Among us is a prophet to whom revelation comes.' By God, we will not accept him unless revelation comes to us just as it comes to him." So it was revealed: ﴿And when a sign comes to them﴾, that is, to the great ones (al-akabir), ﴿a sign﴾, a miracle, or a verse of the Qur'an commanding them to believe, ﴿they say: "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God."﴾ That is, until we are given signs like those given to the prophets. Then God the Exalted informed them that He knows best who is fit for prophethood.

(﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾) Makki and Hafs read "risalatahu" (in the singular). Others read "risalatihi" (in the plural). "Haythu" (where) is the direct object (mafʿul bih), and its governing verb is omitted. The meaning is: He knows the place of His message.

﴿Those who committed crime﴾ among its great ones ﴿will be struck with humiliation (saghar)﴾, meaning disgrace and abasement, ﴿before God﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and a severe punishment﴾ in both abodes, from killing, capture, and the punishment of the Fire, ﴿for what they used to plot﴾ in the world.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 125:**

﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam.﴾ That is, He widens it and illuminates his heart. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the light enters the heart, it expands and opens." It was asked: "What is the sign of that?" He said: "Turning penitently toward the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death arrives."

﴿And whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast constricted﴾ The reading (ḍayyiqan) [with a short vowel, ضَيْقًا] is from Makki, while (ḍayyiqan) [ضَيِّقًا] is from Madani and Abu Bakr. (Ḥarajan) [حَرَجًا] is the reading of the others, used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of an intensifier, meaning "extremely constricted." Its reading as (ḥarijan) [حَرِجًا] is from Madani and Abu Bakr; it is an adjective (ṣifah) of (ḍayyiqan) [ضَيِّقًا].

﴿as if he were climbing up into the sky.﴾ It is as though he were commanded to climb to the sky whenever he is called to Islam, because of the constriction of his breast toward it. Or it means the earth has become too narrow for him, so he seeks a means of ascent into the sky. Or it means: like one who has lost his judgment, a heart flying in the air. The reading (yaṣʿadu) [يَصْعَدُ] is from Makki; (yaṣṣāʿadu) [يَصَّاعَدُ] is from Abu Bakr, and its original form is (yataṣāʿadu) [يَتَصَاعَدُ]; the rest read (yaṣṣaʿʿadu) [يَصَّعَّدُ], and its original form is (yataṣaʿʿadu) [يَتَصَعَّدُ].

﴿Thus Allah places the filth﴾ [i.e., the punishment in the Hereafter, and the curse in this world]

﴿upon those who do not believe.﴾ This verse is a proof for us against the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school that denied that God wills and creates human sinful acts) regarding the will of God over acts of disobedience.

This is the way of your Lord (ṣirāṭ rabbika), that is, His path which wisdom requires, and His practice in expanding the breast of whomever He wills to guide, and making it constricted for whomever He wills to lead astray. Straight (mustaqīman): upright, equitable, consistent. It is a confirming circumstantial state (ḥāl mu'akkidah). We have clearly detailed the signs for a people who take heed (yadhdhakkarūn): who admonish themselves.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 127:

﴿For them﴾, i.e., for a people who take heed. ﴿The abode of peace﴾ is the abode of God, meaning Paradise; He attributed it to Himself to exalt it. Or it is the abode of safety from every calamity and turbidity. Or "peace" (al-salam) means greeting, and it was called "the abode of peace" because of His saying: ﴿Their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10], and ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26]. ﴿With their Lord﴾, in His guarantee, ﴿and He is their Protector (waliyy)﴾, their Beloved (muhibb), or their Helper against their enemies.

﴿For what they used to do﴾, for their deeds; or, He is their Guardian (mutawalli) with the recompense for what they used to do. Or He is our Protector (waliyy) in this world by facilitating deeds, and in the next world by fulfilling hopes.

"And on the Day when He gathers them all" — Ḥafṣ reads it with the yā' (yaḥshuruhum), i.e., "Remember the Day when We gather them," or the phrase is taken as "And on the Day We gather them," [and it is said]: "O assembly of jinn! You have taken a great number from mankind." You misled many of them, and made them your followers, just as one says: "The commander has taken a great number of soldiers." "And their allies among mankind will say," those who obeyed them and listened to their whisperings:

"Our Lord, some of us have enjoyed others" — that is, mankind benefited from the devils, in that they showed them the desires and the means of reaching them; and the jinn benefited from mankind in that they obeyed them and helped them achieve their aims in leading them astray.

"And we have reached our term which You appointed for us" — they mean the Day of Resurrection. This statement is an acknowledgment of what they had done of obeying the devils, following desire, denying the Resurrection, and a lament over their state.

"He will say: The Fire is your abode" — your dwelling place, "wherein you will abide" — this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its governing element (al-'āmil) is the meaning of the annexation (al-iḍāfah), like His saying, exalted is He: "That the cutting off [of the line] of these people is at dawn" [al-Ḥijr: 66]. So "muṣbiḥīn" is a circumstantial clause relating to "hā'ulā'," and the governing element in the circumstantial clause is the meaning of the annexation, since its meaning is "mixing" and "association." The "mathwā" (abode) is not the governing element, because a place does not govern anything. "Except as God wills" — that is, they will be made to abide in the fire of Hell for all of eternity, "except as God wills," except for the times in which they will be transferred from the torment of the blazing fire to the torment of the zamharīr (extreme cold).

"Indeed your Lord is All-Wise" in what He does with His friends and His enemies, "All-Knowing" of their deeds, so He recompenses each according to the measure of his work.

And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others (﴿وَكَذَلِكَ نُوَلِّي بَعْضَ الظالِمِينَ بَعْضًا﴾). We cause some of them to follow others into the Fire, or We give some of them power over others, or We make some of them allies (awliya') of others.

﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ — because of what they had earned (kasb) of disbelief and sins. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, it will be said to them, by way of reproach:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 6, verse 130:

﴿O assembly of jinn and humans, did messengers not come to you from among you?﴾ On the authority of al-Dahhak: He sent messengers to the jinn from among them, just as He sent messengers to humankind from among them, because they are more at ease with them, and the apparent wording of the text supports this. Others said: The messengers were from humankind only. The phrase ﴿messengers from among you﴾ was used because when the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan, i.e. jinn and humans) were addressed together, this phrasing is acceptable even if it applies to only one of them, as in His saying: ﴿From them come forth pearl and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22]. Or their messengers were the messengers of our Prophet, as in His saying: ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. ﴿They recite to you My verses﴾: they read My books. ﴿And warn you of the meeting of this your day﴾: meaning the Day of Resurrection. ﴿They will say: We testify against ourselves﴾: to the establishment of the proof against us and the delivery of the messengers' message to us.

﴿The worldly life deceived them, and they testified against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ in the messengers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 6, verse 131:

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned earlier, the sending of messengers to them. It is the predicate (khabar, the complement of a subject) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), meaning: the matter is that.

﴿That your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people are unaware﴾ is an explanation of cause (ta'lil), meaning: the matter is what We have related to you, because it is not the case that your Lord destroys the towns unjustly. Here "an" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah, forming a verbal noun), but it may also be the lightened form of the heavy "anna" (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and the meaning would be: because the matter and the account ﴿your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly﴾ on account of an injustice they had committed, or as a wrongdoer. This is because, if He had destroyed them while they were unaware, without being warned by a messenger and a Book, He would have been a wrongdoer, and He is exalted above that.

And for each (of the mukallafin, the accountable ones) are ranks (manazil, degrees) according to what they did, meaning the recompense of their deeds. From this verse Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both, derived that the jinn also receive reward for obedience, because it comes right after the mention of the two weighty things (al-thaqalan, humankind and jinn). ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾, meaning not heedless of it. With the ta' (reading "taʿmalūna" with the second person), it is read by Ibn Amir (Shami).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 133:

﴿And your Lord is the Free of need﴾ from His servants and from their worship.

﴿Full of mercy﴾ toward them by imposing obligations (al-taklif), so that He may expose them to lasting benefits.

﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾, O wrongdoers (p-539), ﴿and make whomever He wills succeed you﴾ from among the creatures who are obedient, ﴿just as He produced you from the offspring of another people﴾, from the descendants of other folk who were not of your kind, and they were the people of Noah's ark, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 134:

﴿Indeed, what﴾ "Mā" here means "alladhī" (that which),

﴿you are promised﴾ of the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward, and the punishment,

﴿is coming﴾: the predicate of "inna" (indeed), i.e., it is certainly going to occur.

﴿And you cannot escape﴾: "bi-mu'jizīn" means "not escaping" (bi-fā'itīn). This is a refutation of their saying: "Whoever dies has already escaped."

The Arabic word *al-makanah* can be a verbal noun (*masdar*). It is said: *makana makanatan*, meaning he became firmly established, in the strongest sense of establishment. It can also mean *al-makan* (place). One says *makan*, *makanah*, *maqam* and *maqamah*. His saying, ﴿O my people, act according to your standing﴾, can mean: act according to your firm capacity in your affair and to the utmost of your ability and power, or act according to your direction and the condition you are in. It is said to a man who is commanded to remain in his state: "According to your standing, so-and-so," meaning: remain in what you are upon.

﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ according to my standing, which I hold, meaning: you remain in your disbelief and your enmity toward me, for I remain steadfast in Islam and in my perseverance against you. This is a command of threat and warning. Its evidence is his saying: ﴿Soon you will know to whom the final outcome of the abode belongs﴾, meaning: soon you will know which of us will have the praiseworthy outcome. This is a subtle way of warning. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾, meaning: the disbelievers [will not succeed].

"*Makanatikum*" wherever it occurs: Abu Bakr (read it this way). "*Yakunu*" (in ﴿to whom the final outcome ... belongs﴾, *yakunu*): Hamzah and Ali. The position of "*man*" is nominative (*raf'*) if it means *ayy* ("which"), and the verb of knowledge is suspended from it; or accusative (*nasb*) if it means *alladhi* ("the one who").

(p-٥٤٠)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 136:

﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has created of the crops and cattle﴾, i.e., and for the idols a share. He suffices with the indication of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So they say, "This is for God," by their claim, and this is for our partners.﴾ (By their claim) is an 'Ali (a reading or qualifier), and likewise what follows it; i.e., they claimed that it belongs to God, while God had not commanded them to do that, nor had He prescribed for them that division. ﴿So what is for their partners does not reach God﴾, i.e., it does not reach the purposes to which they used to direct it, such as hospitality for guests and giving charity to the needy.

﴿And what is for God, it reaches their partners﴾ through their spending on them and providing for their attendants (sadana, the custodians of the idols). It is narrated that they used to designate some things from the crops and livestock for God, and some from them for their gods. When they saw that what they had designated for God was growing and thriving, they would transfer it to the idols; and when what they had designated for the idols thrived, they would leave it for them. They would say, "God is self-sufficient," and that was only because of their love for their gods and their preference for them. In His words, ﴿of what He created﴾, there is an indication that God was more entitled to have the thriving portion given to Him, because it is He who created it. Then He censured their conduct with His words, ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾, in preferring their gods over God and in acting upon what had not been prescribed for them. The position of "ma" (what) is in the nominative (raf'), i.e., "evil is the judgment of their judgment"; or in the accusative (nasb), i.e., "evil is the judgment that they judge."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 137:

﴿And thus did their associates make attractive to many of the polytheists﴾ — that is, just as the division of wealth was made attractive to them, the burying of daughters alive was made attractive to them, ﴿the killing﴾ being the object of "made attractive" (zayyana), ﴿of their children by their associates﴾, where "their associates" is the subject of "made attractive."

(zuyyina) with a ḍamma, (qatlu) in the nominative, (awlādahum) in the accusative, and (shurakā'ihim) in the genitive, is the reading of Ibn 'Āmir (al-Shāmī), on the basis of attributing the killing (qatl) to the associates (shurakā'), i.e. the devils (al-shayāṭīn). The separation between them is by something other than an adverbial expression, namely the object. Its construction is: "The killing of their children by their associates was made attractive to many of the polytheists."

﴿So that they might ruin them﴾ — that is, to destroy them through seduction. ﴿And so that they might confuse them regarding their religion﴾ — that is, to mix it up for them and corrupt it. Their religion is what they were upon of the religion of (p-541) Ismā'īl, until they slipped away from it into polytheism. ﴿And had God willed, they would not have done it﴾ — and in this is evidence that all existent things occur by the will of God, exalted is He. ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ — and what they fabricate of falsehood, or their fabrication, because the harm of that fabrication falls upon them, not upon you, nor upon us.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 138:

﴿And they say: "These are cattle and tilth"﴾ for the idols, ﴿forbidden (ḥijr)﴾, meaning prohibited. It is a verbal noun (fi'l) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), like dhibḥ (slaughtered) and ṭiḥn (ground). It applies equally to the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural when used as a description, because its ruling is that of nouns rather than adjectives. When they designated certain things from their tilth and cattle for their gods, they said: ﴿None may eat of it except whom we will, by their claim﴾. They meant: the attendants of the idols and the men, to the exclusion of women. Al-za‛m (claim) is a statement of supposition mixed with falsehood.

﴿And cattle whose backs have been forbidden﴾: these are the baḥā'ir (slit-eared she-camels), the sawā'ib (freed animals), and the ḥawāmī (protected animals).

﴿And cattle over which they do not mention the name of God﴾ at the time of slaughter, but instead they mention over them the names of idols. ﴿Fabricating against Him﴾ is an object of purpose (maf‛ūl lahu) or a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: they divided their cattle into three kinds: a kind that is ḥijr, a kind that is not ridden, and a kind over which the name of God is not mentioned, and they attributed this to God, fabricating against Him. ﴿He will recompense them for what they have been fabricating﴾: this is a threat.

﴿And they say: "What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives."﴾ They used to say about the fetuses of the baheera and the sa'iba: whatever is born of them alive is exclusively for the males, and females may not eat of it, but whatever is born dead, males and females share in it. "Khālisa" is feminine, and it is the predicate of "mā," in agreement with the meaning (al-ḥaml ʿalā al-maʿnā, "agreement according to sense"), because "mā" here means "the fetuses." "Muḥarram" is masculine, in agreement with the wording (al-ḥaml ʿalā al-lafẓ), or the "tāʾ" is for emphasis (lil-mubālagha), as in "nassāba" (a person who very often traces lineages).

﴿And if it is dead (yakun maytatan)﴾: that is, ﴿and if it is﴾ what is in their wombs "dead." (Wa-in takun maytatan) Abu Bakr [reads it thus], [p. 542] meaning: and if the fetuses are dead. (Wa-in takun maytatun) [is read by] al-Shami, with "kāna" as a complete verb (kāna al-tāmma, "kāna" used without a predicate in the sense of "to occur/exist"). (Yakun maytatun) [is read by] al-Makki, because the verb is placed first (li-taqaddum al-fiʿl, "because the verb precedes").

The pronoun in ﴿they are partners in it﴾ is masculine because "maytah" is a noun for every dead thing, male or female. It is as if it were said: "And if there is a dead [offspring], they are partners in it."

﴿He will repay them for their description﴾: He will repay them for their description, that is, for their lying about Allah concerning what is permitted and forbidden. ﴿Indeed He is Wise﴾ in their recompense, ﴿Knowing﴾ of their belief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 140:

﴿Indeed, they have lost who have killed their children﴾ They used to bury their daughters alive (wa'd), out of fear of captivity and poverty. (qattalū) is the reading of Ibn Kathir (Makki) and of the Syrian readers (Shami).

﴿in ignorance, foolishly﴾ due to the lightness of their intellects and their ignorance that Allah is the provider of their children, not they themselves. ﴿And they have forbidden what Allah has provided for them﴾ from the baḥā'ir, the sawā'ib, and others.

﴿as a fabrication against Allah﴾ is a maf'ūl lahu (object of purpose).

﴿Indeed they have gone astray and were not guided﴾ to what is correct.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 141:**

﴿It is He who produced﴾ created ﴿gardens﴾ of vines ﴿trellised﴾ (*maskūkāt*), raised up (*marfū'āt*).

﴿And [He produced] those not trellised﴾ left (*matrūkāt*) on the surface of the earth, not trellised. It is said: "I trellised the vine" (*'arrashtu al-karm*) when you make supports and a framework for it, so that the shoots are trained over it.

﴿And the palm trees and crops, differing﴾ in color, taste, size and fragrance. This is an anticipated circumstantial clause (*ḥāl muqaddara*), because at the time the palm tree emerges there is no fruit to eat, so that it could be "differing." It is like His saying: ﴿Enter them to abide therein﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. "*Ukuluhu*" (*ukluhu*) is the Hijazi reading, and it means its fruit that is eaten; the pronoun refers to the palm tree. The crops fall under its ruling, because they are conjoined to it, or [the pronoun refers] to each one of them.

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, similar﴾ in color, ﴿and dissimilar﴾ in taste. ﴿Eat of its fruit﴾, of the fruit of each of them. The benefit of ﴿when it bears fruit﴾ is to make known that the first time of permission is the time the tree puts forth fruit, and it should not be imagined that it is not permitted except when it has ripened. ﴿And give its due﴾ its tithe. This is the proof of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, for the generality of the tithe (p-543) ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾: "*ḥaṣādihi*" (*ḥaṣādihi*, with fatḥa on the ḥā') is Basri, Shami and ʿĀṣim's reading; with kasra on the ḥā' it is the reading of the others. They are two dialects.

﴿And do not be extravagant﴾ by giving away everything and neglecting dependents. His saying ﴿Eat…﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tirāḍ*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 142:

﴿And of the cattle, [He produced] beasts of burden and [animals for] flesh (furash).﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with "gardens" (jannat), meaning: He produced from the cattle that which carries loads and that which is laid down for slaughter (yuftarash li-l-dhabh). Or, al-ḥamūlah are the large ones fit for carrying, and al-farsh are the young ones, such as the weaned camels (al-fiṣlān), the calves (al-ʿajājīl), and the sheep and goats (al-ghanam), because they are close to the ground, like the spread-out carpet (al-farsh al-mafrūsh) laid upon it. ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ meaning: of what He has made lawful (uḥilla) for you from them, and do not forbid them as was done in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ meaning: his ways in declaring things lawful and unlawful, like the practice of the people of the Jahiliyyah. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ so distrust him regarding your religion.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 143:**

﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾ (*thamaniyata azwajin*, "eight pairs") is in apposition (*badal*, a grammatical substitution) for ﴿حَمُولَةً وفَرْشًا﴾ ("[animals for] burden and [animals for] flat [i.e., small] cattle"). ﴿مِنَ الضَأْنِ اثْنَيْنِ ومِنَ المَعْزِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ ("two of the sheep and two of the goats"), meaning two pairs: ﴿اثْنَيْنِ﴾ ("two") refers to the male and the female. A single animal on its own is a *fard* (an odd, single one), but when it has another of its kind with it, each of the two is called a *zawj* (a mate, one of a pair), and the two together are *zawjan*. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿خَلَقَ الزَوْجَيْنِ الذَكَرَ والأُنْثى﴾ ("He created the two mates, the male and the female") [An-Najm: 45]. His saying ﴿ثَمانِيَةَ أزْواجٍ﴾ indicates this, and then He explained it with His saying: ﴿مِنَ الضَأْنِ اثْنَيْنِ ومِنَ المَعْزِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ ﴿وَمِنَ الإبِلِ اثْنَيْنِ ومِنَ البَقَرِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ ("and of the camels two, and of the cattle two").

*Al-Dda'n* (sheep) and *al-Ma'z* (goats) are plurals of *da'in* and *ma'iz*, like *tajir* and *tajr* (a merchant and merchants). The reading of the ʿayn in *al-Ma'az* (with a fatha, *al-Ma'az*) is that of Makki, Shami and Abu ʿAmr; both forms are dialectal variants (*lughatan*).

The hamza in ﴿قُلْ آلذَّكَرَيْنِ حَرَّمَ أمِ الأُنْثَيَيْنِ أمّا اشْتَمَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ أرْحامُ الأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ ("Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain?") is an interrogative of denial (*li'l-inkar*). By "the two males" is meant the male of the sheep and the male of the goat; by "the two females" is meant the female of the sheep and the female of the goat. The meaning is a denial that God has forbidden, from the two species of the flock, sheep and goats, any part of the males or females of either kind, nor anything that the females carry. This is because they used to forbid the males of the livestock at one time, the females at another, and their offspring, whether male, female or mixed, at yet another time, and they would say: "God has forbidden it." So He denied this against them (p-544). ﴿آلذَّكَرَيْنِ﴾ ("the two males") is in the accusative governed by ﴿حَرَّمَ﴾ ("has forbidden"); likewise ﴿أمِ الأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ means "or has He forbidden the two females?" and likewise what follows in ﴿أمّا اشْتَمَلَتْ﴾ ("or what [the wombs] contain").

﴿نَبِّئُونِي بِعِلْمٍ﴾ ("Inform me with knowledge") means: tell me with a matter known from God's side that indicates the prohibition of what you have forbidden ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ ("if you are truthful") in the claim that God has forbidden it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 144:

﴿And of camels two, and of cattle two. Say: Has He forbidden the two males, or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ [He forbade] of them [both].

﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ "Or" (am) here is disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning: "Rather, were you witnesses?"

﴿when God enjoined this upon you?﴾ That is: Did you witness your Lord when He commanded you this prohibition? Since they did not believe in the Messenger of God, and they would say, "God has forbidden what we forbid," He mocked them with His words: ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾ in the sense of: Did you know of the enjoining of it as onlookers, since you do not believe in the messengers?

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God﴾ so that he attributes to Him the prohibition of what He did not prohibit, ﴿to lead people astray without knowledge? Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ That is: those who, in His knowledge, will die upon disbelief.
